target: AG1’s claim that a federal Election Day holiday would “give people a day off to go to the polls” and directly remove scheduling barriers
objection: Designating Election Day as a federal holiday would not reliably give most people paid time off or a day off from work, because U.S. federal holiday status generally does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave. As a result, many workers—especially low-income hourly workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs—would still work and still face the same timing constraints, so the holiday would not actually solve the scheduling problem for them.

target: AG1’s assumption that a national holiday would substantially increase access to voting more effectively than other reforms
objection: An election-day holiday is a weak and uncertain turnout reform compared with measures that directly change voting logistics, such as expanded early voting, easier absentee/mail voting, or automatic voter registration. Because it does not itself alter those mechanisms, its effect on turnout is less reliable than more targeted access reforms.

target: AG2’s objection that a federal holiday would not change real-world schedules because private employers need not close
objection: A national Election Day holiday would still reduce scheduling barriers because it changes the actual calendar that shapes schools, childcare, and many workplaces, not just legal employer obligations. Schools generally close on national holidays, many workplaces follow holiday schedules or grant time off in practice, and that gives millions of voters—especially parents and caregivers—daytime availability to vote even if not every private employer is required to close.

target: AG1’s broader assumption that holiday status would meaningfully change daytime availability for most voters
objection: Even if some schools close, a federal holiday does not legally require private employers to close or pay workers, so millions of hourly workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and other sectors would still have to work. For low-income workers facing the tightest time constraints, the main obstacle would remain in place, so a holiday is not a reliable scheduling solution.

target: AG2’s claim that only direct voting-logistics reforms address the problem
objection: The scheduling barrier includes school and childcare constraints, not just employer rules. If Election Day is a national holiday, schools close and childcare arrangements shift, which directly helps parents and caregivers who otherwise must choose between voting and their daytime responsibilities. So the holiday does address a major part of the timing problem.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would improve access for many people by changing schools and workplace schedules
objection: Research and experience suggest that an election-day-only holiday is a weak turnout strategy by itself; it does not directly change the key barriers that keep people from voting, especially for working people. More effective reforms are those that explicitly reduce voting friction, such as employer time-off laws or automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s preference for a holiday over targeted reforms
objection: State laws requiring employers to provide time off for voting, and automatic voter registration, are more reliable solutions than a federal holiday. They directly address the relevant barriers—time off and registration—rather than assuming a holiday will indirectly improve access.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would be a reliable “day available” for voting
objection: The argument assumes that holiday designation will actually make workplaces and school/childcare schedules change in practice for most constrained voters, but that is not guaranteed. Because private employers are not required to close or offer paid leave, and childcare routines may not shift uniformly nationwide, a national holiday does not reliably create a society-wide day off for voting.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not reliably create time off because employer closure is not mandated
objection: The decisive issue is not only whether every private employer must close, but whether the holiday changes the real-world scheduling environment enough to let many working and parenting households vote. Since many workplaces follow holiday schedules and schools/childcare arrangements shift, the holiday still creates a broad day of availability and thus directly addresses the scheduling barrier.

target: AG2’s objection that low-income workers would still be scheduled and therefore would not benefit meaningfully
objection: The holiday would help precisely because the main obstacle is not just employer mandates in the abstract; it is the need to coordinate work, school, childcare, and transportation during a limited in-person voting window. By changing the day structure that governs those routines, Election Day as a holiday creates a practical opportunity to vote that the current schedule does not provide.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is uniquely suited to helping people most harmed by work and school schedules
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee that school and childcare routines will shift uniformly or that private employers will provide time off, so it does not reliably produce a society-wide day available for voting. Because the most constrained voters can still be working or otherwise tied to their usual routines, the holiday is not uniquely suited to the scheduling barrier in the way claimed.
